title: The Printing Press
objective: After this level you can explain how Gutenberg's press made books cheap and spread ideas.
summary: Gutenberg combined metal type, oil-based ink and a press. Movable type began in China and Korea, but his system took Europe from thousands of books to over 9 million by 1500.

cards.headline: Before printing, Europe had thousands of books. By 1500: over 9 million.
cards.body: Every one of those older books had been copied out by hand. Then, in only about 50 years, Europe went from thousands of books to millions. What changed was a machine, and it was really three inventions working as one.

cards.headline: Three inventions in one workshop
cards.body: Gutenberg's system had three parts. Metal type: separate letters cast from an alloy that melts easily and cools fast, tough enough to reuse. An oil-based ink, thick enough to cling to metal and print cleanly on paper. And a press, probably adapted from the ones used for wine, oil or paper, to squeeze each sheet down firmly and evenly. Set a page once, and you could print it again and again.

cards.fact: Gutenberg didn't invent movable type. He built the machine around it.
cards.context: In China, Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay in 1041-48. Korea was printing with metal type in the 14th century. Gutenberg's feat was Europe's first known mechanized printing press, which made books far cheaper to produce. Level 1's timeline puts his Bible at about 1455.

cards.headline: When an idea outruns its author
cards.body: Martin Luther dated his 95 theses October 31, 1517. They were arguments for a scholarly debate at Wittenberg, and he didn't hand them out to the public. Others translated them into German and had them printed. Thanks to the press, they were known throughout Germany within a few weeks. Hand copying moved at the speed of a pen. Printing let an idea travel faster than the person who wrote it.

mascot.line: Luther wrote for a small debate. The printers invited everyone else.

questions.prompt: Which three parts made up Gutenberg's printing system?

options.label: Clay type, water-based ink and a loom
options.rationale: Clay type was Bi Sheng's, and there was no loom.

options.label: Reusable metal type, oil-based ink and a press
Carved wood blocks, paint and a roller
options.rationale: His letters were cast in metal.

options.label: Quill pens, parchment and a team of copyists
options.rationale: That's the hand copying printing replaced.

questions.explanation: Gutenberg cast reusable metal type, used a thick oil-based ink that clung to it, and pressed each sheet in a press adapted from wine, oil or paper presses.

questions.prompt: Luther meant his 95 theses for a debate at Wittenberg. How were they known across Germany within weeks?

options.label: Luther mailed handwritten copies to every town
options.rationale: He didn't hand them out to the public at all.

options.label: Church bells announced them in every city
options.rationale: Bells don't carry arguments; printed copies did.

options.label: Others translated them and had them printed
A telegraph line carried them from Wittenberg
options.rationale: The telegraph came more than 300 years later.

questions.explanation: Others translated the theses into German and printed them, and printing made them known throughout Germany within a few weeks.

questions.prompt: Level 1 called technology knowledge put to work on a practical job. What job did Gutenberg's press do far better than copying by hand?

options.label: Inventing movable type for the first time
options.rationale: China and Korea had movable type first.

options.label: Writing brand-new books by itself
options.rationale: People still had to write the books.

options.label: Printing the same page again and again

questions.explanation: Once a page was set in reusable metal type, the press could print it over and over, making books far cheaper than hand copies.
